03 / BEYOND THE HEADCOUNT

What does everyday life look like?

Literacy, schooling and household conditions offer different views of opportunity.

MICS describes a sample-based estimate for a defined population. Different ages, denominators and reference windows cannot be combined into one trend.

04 / STAYING, LEAVING, RETURNING

Climate changes the choices.
It does not explain every move.

Education, work, family, housing and environmental risks interact. The evidence is stronger for these pathways than for a single “climate migration rate.”

A POSSIBLE PATHWAY · NOT A CAUSAL ESTIMATE

Changing climate & hazardsFloods · glacial lake outbursts · disrupted water
↓
Pressure on daily lifeHomes · roads · crops · income · schooling
↓
Different household responsesAdapt locally · move temporarily · relocate · return

Not everyone can or wants to move. Resources and social networks shape the available choices.

05 / TRANSPARENCY IS PART OF THE RESULT

What we know.
What we still need.

Every chart is an argument. Here are the limits of ours.

Download the research review ↓
DISPUTED 1951 and 2017 totals

1951 appears as 252,000 or 254,000. The yearbook gives 1,492,924 and 1,492,685 for 2017. Both versions remain available. We do not average them.

MISSING An observed 2025 total

No observed 2025 population was verified. An ambiguously dated projection of 1,748,769 is excluded from the chart. The study period ends in 2025; that does not mean a census exists for 2025.

MISSING Youth migration rates & destinations

No representative GB-wide series establishing how many young people moved to each city or country was validated. National emigration counts cannot substitute for GB-specific data.

METHOD CHANGE Survey comparisons

The older and newer MICS mortality estimates use different methods. Fertility reference windows also differ. Point-estimate differences are not automatically statistically significant.

UNRESOLVED District boundaries & causality

Reporting units need a historical geographic crosswalk. Population growth alone cannot identify migration, climate effects, or improvements in quality of life.
